_comment: Describes this standalone build for ../lesson-app-tools/. Wired to the platform shell since 2026-09-18 by wire-platform.py, NOT the shared wire-progress.py / wire-platform-controls.py G1-4 use - this build has no deck, no finish(), no .dots nav, so those two refuse outright. Progress here means 'section reached': an IntersectionObserver over each lesson's <section class="step"> blocks, unit.completed firing once every section has been seen - the closest honest equivalent to G1-4's last finish() on a page with no check to pass. See check-platform-wiring.py. index.html is a real hub of six cards, generated with the lesson pages by split-into-lessons.py; squares-and-steps.html is that generator's INPUT and is deliberately not listed here, so it is not shipped.
subject: mathematics

lessons.title: Squares, Cubes and Roots
lessons.materials: About 30 small cubes or counters to build a physical square (4 rows of 4) and then a solid cube (a 3 by 3 by 3 stack), plus squared paper for drawing the growing L shapes. Stacking a real cube is what makes cubing a number mean something more than a repeated multiplication.
lessons.support: If the L shapes are confusing, go back to counting the WHOLE square each time rather than just the new dots: 9, then 16, then 25. Once the totals feel secure, come back and count only the new dots that were added.
lessons.challenge: A square number is never one more than a multiple of 4, except 1 itself — 4²=16, 5²=25, 6²=36. Pick five square numbers and check whether that rule holds. Can you see why it must, from the odd-number L shapes?

lessons.title: Rules and Patterns
lessons.materials: Matchsticks, toothpicks or straws to build the first few terms of a growing pattern by hand, and squared paper to record how many are used each time. Building pattern 1, 2 and 3 for real is what makes the jump to pattern 10 a rule rather than a guess.
lessons.support: Make a table with two columns, Pattern number and How many, and fill in only the patterns you can actually build and count — 1, 2, 3. Look at how much the second column grows each time before trying to jump ahead to pattern 10.
lessons.challenge: Every pattern in this lesson grows by the same amount each time. Invent your own pattern that grows by a DIFFERENT amount each step — for example, add 1 more than last time. Can you still find a rule for the 10th term?

lessons.title: How Whole Numbers Are Built
lessons.materials: A place-value grid (or squared paper ruled into columns) for writing big numbers digit by digit, and a calculator for checking multiplication and division by hand first. Seeing a digit sit in its own column is what stops "the value of a digit" being an abstract rule.
lessons.support: Before working with a big number, write it into a place-value grid one digit per box, labelling each column (ones, tens, hundreds...) as you go. Point to the digit you are asked about and read its column's label out loud before answering.
lessons.challenge: Take any 4-digit number and rearrange its digits to make the biggest possible number, then the smallest. What is the difference between them? Try it with a different starting number — does the same column always end up mattering most?

lessons.title: Past the Whole Numbers
lessons.materials: A number line marked in tenths and hundredths (or a metre ruler, read as a decimal number line) for placing and rounding decimals. Pointing to where 3.7 actually sits is what makes rounding a matter of nearness rather than a rule about the digit after the point.
lessons.support: Before rounding a decimal, mark it on a number line between its two nearest whole numbers first — 3.7 goes between 3 and 4. Look at which one it sits closer to before deciding which way to round.
lessons.challenge: Find a decimal that rounds to 6 at the nearest whole number, to 6.0 at the nearest tenth, AND to 6.00 at the nearest hundredth, all at once. How many different decimals could you have picked?

lessons.title: Real Life
lessons.support: Before choosing an answer, underline the question being asked and circle every number in the story. Say the story back in your own words, leaving the numbers out, so you are sure what is actually happening before you calculate.
lessons.challenge: Pick any problem from this lesson and change one number in it, so the story still makes sense but the answer changes. Work out your own new answer — does the SAME method from the original problem still get you there?

lessons.title: Shapes and Angles
lessons.blurb: Classify triangles by side and symmetry, name an angle by eye, use 180 degrees on a straight line, separate perimeter from area, cut a compound shape into rectangles, fold a net into a cube, and complete a symmetrical pattern.
lessons.support: Start with the corner of a piece of paper as your right angle. Hold it against each angle in the lesson and say only whether the angle is smaller or bigger than the corner - acute or obtuse - before worrying about the number of degrees.
lessons.challenge: Every rectangle in Step 32 has whole-number sides. Find the rectangle with perimeter 24 that has the LARGEST area, then try perimeter 20 and perimeter 36. What shape does the biggest-area rectangle always turn out to be, and why?
lessons.materials: A ruler, and a sheet of squared paper for the perimeter and area work. The corner of any piece of paper is a ready-made right angle for testing whether an angle is acute or obtuse. For the nets, six paper squares taped edge to edge, or a small cardboard box cut open along its edges and laid flat - folding a real one is what makes an arrangement that cannot fold obvious.

lessons.title: Where Things Are and How They Move
lessons.blurb: Read and plot coordinate pairs, find a point on a grid with no gridlines, translate a shape and describe a translation someone else made, and reflect a shape in a vertical or horizontal mirror line.
lessons.materials: Squared paper, and a ruler or any straight edge - the straight edge is what makes the no-gridlines step work, because you line it up from the point to each axis. A small cut-out triangle is worth having for the translation step: sliding a real one across the paper shows that it never turns.
lessons.support: Say the order out loud every time: along the corridor, then up the stairs. Do that before writing either number down, and the commonest mistake in this whole lesson - giving the pair the wrong way round - cannot happen.
lessons.challenge: In Step 41, reflect the shape in the vertical mirror, then reflect the RESULT in the horizontal mirror. Where does it end up, and is there a single translation or rotation that would have taken the original there in one move?
